learn.title: Same size, different input
learn.body: Two arrays of the same length can cost an algorithm different amounts of work. The best case is the input that makes it cheapest. The worst case is the input that makes it cost the most. Worst case is the safe number to plan with.

learn.title: Scanning for a target
learn.body: This loop stops when it finds `t`. We count the loop passes in `steps`.

learn.title: Three runs on {7, 3, 9, 1, 5}
learn.body: The array has 5 items. Count the passes for three targets.
steps: Target 7 is first: 1 pass. This is the best case
Target 5 is last: 5 passes, the worst case
Target 4 is not in the array: also 5 passes
So the work is between 1 and n: $\Omega(1)$ and $O(n)$

learn.title: Cases versus bounds
learn.body: Best and worst case describe inputs. O, omega and theta describe growth. They are different tools. You can say the worst case is $\Theta(n)$ and the best case is $\Theta(1)$. Each case has its own tight bound.

learn.title: The average case
learn.body: The average case is the typical cost over all inputs. It is harder to work out, because you must say what typical means. For this scan, if the target is equally likely to be anywhere, you look at about half the items on average.
When you hear that an algorithm is fast, ask: in which case? Many are fast on easy input and slow on hard input.

questions.prompt: In the scan, what is the best case?
choices: The target is the first item
The target is the last item
questions.explanation: Finding the target immediately takes 1 pass.

questions.prompt: Array of 5 items. The target is the last item. How many passes does the scan make?
questions.explanation: The target is only found on pass 5, the last one.

questions.prompt: Array of 5 items. The target is not in the array. How many passes?
questions.explanation: The scan must check every item before it knows the target is missing.

questions.prompt: What is the worst case of the scan, in big O?
questions.explanation: Up to n passes for n items.

questions.prompt: The \_\_ case is the input that makes an algorithm do the most work.
questions.explanation: Worst case gives the upper limit you can rely on.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to its case for the scan.
questions.explanation: Case describes the input, not the algorithm's code.

choices: Best case and worst case are properties of inputs
Theta only exists for the worst case
questions.explanation: The cases pick an input. The bounds describe how a count grows.
